title: Vietnamese Thien
hookLine: Thien joins Chan with Pure Land chanting, as in much of Vietnam

lines: NAM MÔ A DI ĐÀ PHẬT.
cards: Evening at a pagoda in Vietnam. The incense is lit. A small bell sounds, and the hall, monks and nuns at the front, lay families behind, begins to chant together.

Over and over, one line rises: Nam mô A Di Đà Phật. Then the chanting stops, and the same people sit in silence, eyes lowered. Some visitors expect one or the other, a Zen temple or a temple of devotion.
In much of Vietnam, the hall holds both. Today: Vietnamese Thien.

teach.b: First, the name. You met Thien once before, when Chan came to Vietnam. It's the Vietnamese way of saying the word that is Chan in China, Seon in Korea and Zen in Japan: same character, four pronunciations.
Second, the two streams. Thien is the meditation stream we've followed for weeks.
Pure Land is a different emphasis: devotion to Amitabha Buddha, A Di Đà in Vietnamese, and the hope, in Pure Land teaching, of rebirth in his Pure Land through calling his name with trust.

teach.h: NAM MÔ A DI ĐÀ PHẬT.
teach.b: Nam mô A Di Đà Phật means homage to Amitabha Buddha. In much of Vietnam, the two flow together, in the same temples and often in one person's practice. Third, how they fit.

teach.h: CHANTING AS A DOOR TO SITTING.
teach.b: Some teachers say chanting the name steadies the mind the way counting breaths does, a door into sitting. Others put it the other way: sitting clears the mind, so the name is said with a whole heart.
Pure Land teachers hold that the name has power of its own, through Amitabha's vow. In Vietnamese temples these views sit side by side, without being forced into one. Fourth, a modern voice.
Thich Nhat Hanh, a Vietnamese Thien teacher who taught in Vietnam and the West, spoke of mindfulness in chanting, walking, eating, even the sound of a bell.
In his communities, when a bell rings, people pause and come back to the breath: sound, then silence.

how: In Vietnamese temples, evening services often join chanting, including the name of Amitabha Buddha (Nam mô A Di Đà Phật), with periods of silent sitting, and lay families often take part alongside monks and nuns.

o: a Vietnamese school that keeps chanting out of the hall
the silent retreat season in Vietnamese temples
Vietnam's Chan, often practiced alongside Pure Land chanting

p: Nam mô A Di Đà Phật
mindfulness at the sound of a bell

s: in Vietnam, Thien meditation and Pure Land chanting often share one temple
the same hall can hold the chant and the silent sit.
Thien and Zen are unrelated words
they're the same word, read in Vietnamese and Japanese, along with Chan and Seon.
Nam mô A Di Đà Phật means 'I am the Buddha'
it means homage to Amitabha Buddha.

games.q: you visit a Vietnamese pagoda expecting either a silent Zen hall or a chanting service. what do you find?
o: chanting, then sitting, in the same hall.
games.why: in much of Vietnam, the two streams flow together: the name of Amitabha is chanted, and then the hall sits in silence.

practice: If you're comfortable with it, say the line from today's hall slowly three times, softly or silently, letting it fill the out-breath: Nam mô A Di Đà Phật, homage to Amitabha Buddha.
If you'd rather not chant, listen to your own breathing as if it were a bell. Then let the sound go, and sit in the quiet it leaves behind.

wordCard.voice: Vietnamese Thien. The Chan meditation stream as it lives in Vietnam, often practiced side by side with Pure Land chanting of Amitabha Buddha's name. Today's word.

orig.note: Vietnamese: Thiền, the same character 禪 read as Chan in Chinese, Seon in Korean, Zen in Japanese. Pronunciation is approximate; Vietnamese is tonal.

carryVoice: Your line: sit and chant. In one hall, the voice and the stillness both belong. See you tomorrow.
